title: A bootstrap band asks how much the fitted curve could move if the measurements had been slightly different
summary: Eight measured ignition delays are joined by an interpolating curve. To show how uncertain that curve is, the data are perturbed by a small random jitter many times and re-interpolated. The band is where 95 percent of those re-interpolated curves lie. It is wide where the curve has little support and narrow where points constrain it.

media.alt: Ethyl butanoate ignition delay in milliseconds on a log axis against temperature from about 685 to 820 K. Eight dark blue dots are measurements, a smooth blue mean curve passes through them, and a light blue 95 percent band is wide at the cold end, narrow near 740 K, and widens again at the hot end. Dashed vertical lines mark regions labelled pre-NTC, NTC and post-NTC.

source.caption: Chapter 3. Ethyl butanoate ignition delay vs temperature near 3 MPa: 8 measured points, spline mean curve, 95% bootstrap interval
source.note: Two small Chapter 3 figures that turn a handful of ignition-delay measurements into a smooth curve with an uncertainty band, by resampling with a 2 percent jitter. The same panel is drawn for ethyl butanoate (8 points, spline mean) and methyl butanoate (7 points, PCHIP mean). The generated curves are used as stand-in targets, so the figure is about the data, not about any mechanism.

read_the_figure.question: Given the few measurements, how well is the ignition-delay curve determined at each temperature?
read_the_figure.axes: x: temperature in kelvin (not 1000/T here). y: ignition delay in milliseconds on a log scale. Dots: measurements. Thick line: mean of the regenerated curves. Shaded band: central 95 percent of the regenerated curves at each temperature. Dashed lines: boundaries of the pre-NTC, NTC and post-NTC regions.
look_at: Where the band is narrow, the interpolated curve is pinned by nearby points. In figure 09 this is near the minimum at about 740 K.
Where the band flares, there is little data and the interpolation is free to swing. The cold-end flare in figure 09 and the hot-end flare near the last point are boundary effects of the interpolant.

In figure 09 the band is widest at the cold end, where the curve is steep and the first points are far apart, so a 2 percent change in one point moves the curve a lot. A steep log-scale curve turns small horizontal and vertical uncertainties into large band widths.
Check that every measured dot lies inside the band. A dot outside means the generated curves do not represent the data.

Compare figures 09 and 10. The methyl butanoate panel has a much narrower band along an almost straight, monotonic curve. The curvature of the underlying data, not the amount of jitter, sets the width.
read_the_figure.proves: That the generated target curve is stable against a 2 percent perturbation of the points, to within the band. It does not show the experiment's own uncertainty, which is not what was resampled.
if_wrong: Band as narrow as the line everywhere: too little jitter, or too few resamples to see the spread.
Band excludes measured points: the interpolation is overshooting between points, or the jitter is too small relative to scatter.
Band flares wildly at the ends: the interpolant extrapolates. Do not use targets near the ends without a wider uncertainty.
A mean curve that differs visibly from a curve through the original points: a bias from an asymmetric jitter.
must_check: The number of bootstrap replicates is stated (500).
The jitter size and whether it is relative (2 percent here).
What is being resampled: the measurements, not the model.
The band is not confused with the experimental error bars of the underlying data.

terms.meaning: Resampling or perturbing the data many times and recomputing a statistic each time, to see how much the statistic varies.
One random draw of the jittered data and the curve fitted to it. B = 500 replicates are drawn.
A small random perturbation added to each measurement before refitting.
The band between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the replicates at each x.
A curve forced to pass through every measured point: here a spline for one fuel and a monotone piecewise cubic (PCHIP) for the other.
Temperatures in which the delay increases as temperature rises. It is the middle section of the curve here.
A confidence band is about the curve, a prediction band is about a new observation. A bootstrap of the fit gives the first.

remember: A bootstrap band measures the stability of a procedure, not truth.
The band is the spread of curves, not of data.
More replicates make the band edges smoother, not wider.
Wide at the ends is a property of interpolation.
The jitter is an assumption: the band scales with it.

steps.title: Perturb the data
steps.note: One replicate: every measured delay is multiplied by a random factor within about two percent. The figure's titles give the size and the number of replicates; that the jitter is multiplicative is an assumption.

steps.title: Refit the curve for every replicate
steps.note: The same interpolation method (spline or PCHIP) is applied to each jittered data set, giving B curves.

steps.title: Summarise at each temperature
steps.note: The thick line is the mean of the replicates and the band is their central 95 percent. This is the percentile bootstrap interval.

steps.title: How the position of the band edge is found
steps.note: With B = 500 the lower edge is between the 12th and 13th smallest replicate values at that temperature, and the upper edge between the 487th and 488th. Sort the 500 values and read them off.

steps.title: Gaussian check
steps.note: If the replicates at one temperature are roughly normal with standard deviation s, the band width is about 3.92 s. This gives a quick sanity check against the drawn width.

steps.title: Why Monte Carlo error is not the band
steps.note: The mean curve's own Monte Carlo error falls as one over the square root of B, so 500 replicates give about 4.5 percent of s. This is separate from the width of the band, which stays put as B grows.

worked.title: Locating the band edges for B = 500
worked.problem: At one temperature the 500 replicate delays are sorted. Which ranked values give the 95 percent percentile band, and how large is the Monte Carlo error of the mean relative to the replicate standard deviation?

solution.text: Error of the mean relative to s.

worked.answer: Take values ranked 12 and 13 (average them) for the lower edge and 487 and 488 for the upper edge. The mean curve's own Monte Carlo error is about 4.5 percent of the replicate spread. Both numbers follow from B = 500, which the figure prints.

analyze.q: Why is the band in figure 09 wide at the cold end even though the jitter is only two percent?
analyze.hint: Think about what the interpolant does between the first two points and beyond the first point.

analyze.q: If the jitter were doubled, would the band exactly double in width? What would break that proportionality?
analyze.hint: Nonlinearity of the interpolant, and the log scale of the axis.

analyze.q: Which of the two figures would give a more reliable target for an optimization, and why?
analyze.hint: Compare narrow monotonic with wide curved.

evaluate.q: Is a 2 percent jitter a good stand-in for experimental uncertainty? What would you use instead?
evaluate.hint: The reported uncertainties of the measurements, per point.

evaluate.q: Would you describe the band as a 95 percent confidence band for the true ignition delay? Why or why not?
evaluate.hint: What is and is not being resampled.

create: Redraw both panels on 1000/T axes with the original error bars of the measurements as well as the bootstrap band, in different tints.
Design a leave-one-point-out test that shows which measured point the flare at the cold end depends on.

checks.q: What is resampled in this figure?
checks.answer: The measured delays are perturbed by a small random jitter and the curve is refitted each time. The model and the experiment are not rerun.

checks.q: For B = 500 replicates, which ranks give a 95 percent percentile interval?
checks.answer: About ranks 12.5 and 487.5: average values 12 and 13 and values 487 and 488.

checks.q: Why does the band flare at the ends of the temperature range?
checks.hint: What constrains the curve at the ends?
checks.answer: Only one neighbouring point constrains the curve at an end, so a small change of that point swings the interpolant and extrapolation beyond it. In the interior, points on both sides pin it.

checks.q: Two bands have the same width but one is drawn with B = 50 and one with B = 5000. Which would you trust?
checks.hint: Monte Carlo error of the edges.
checks.answer: The 5000-replicate band: its percentile edges are much less noisy. The widths are about equal because they reflect the data and the jitter, not B.

checks.q: How would you build a band that also reflects the experiment's own scatter?
checks.answer: Draw each replicate from a normal distribution centred on the measurement with its own reported standard deviation (in the log), refit, and take percentiles. That replaces the single global 2 percent with measured uncertainty.
